before.title: 1.5L Turbo PCV System Failure and Coolant/Oil Intrusion
before.description: The 2018+ Terrain with the 1.5L turbocharged engine (LFV/LYX) experiences PCV (Positive Crankcase Ventilation) diaphragm failure inside the valve cover. The integrated PCV diaphragm tears, causing excessive crankcase pressure that forces oil into the intake manifold and intercooler. before.title: Engine-Driven Brake Vacuum Pump Failure - Sudden Loss of Power Brake Assist (Hard Pedal)
before.description: On second-generation Terrains (2018-2022) with the 1.5L LYX and 2.0L LTG turbo engines, the camshaft-driven mechanical vacuum pump that supplies the brake booster can fail suddenly and without warning. When it fails, drivers lose power brake assist and the pedal becomes hard as a rock, requiring dramatically increased effort to stop and greatly increasing crash risk. In severe cases pump internals disintegrate and send metal debris into the engine oil, contaminating internal components and turning a brake repair into a costly engine job. The defect is the subject of a February 18, 2026 proposed federal class-action (Thieme, Gill, Morley v. General Motors, LLC, E.D. Michigan) covering 2018-2022 Equinox/Terrain and 2016-2020 Buick Envision; the suit alleges GM knew of the issue as early as a March 2017 stop-delivery order. No recall has been issued as of mid-2026.
before.solution: Replace the failed camshaft-driven vacuum pump (and the brake booster if it was damaged). If the pump disintegrated, an oil-system flush and inspection for metal contamination is required; catastrophic cases need internal engine repair. With no recall issued, repairs are typically owner-paid unless covered by powertrain warranty or resolved through the pending class action.
symptoms: Brake pedal suddenly hard/stiff and difficult to press
Whining or knocking noise from front of engine
Metal shavings in engine oil in severe cases

before.title: Throttle Body / Throttle Position Sensor Failure - 'Reduced Engine Power' Warning
before.description: First-generation Terrains (2010-2017) are prone to a sudden 'Reduced Engine Power' warning caused by a failing electronic throttle body. Carbon and grime build up inside the bore and the internal throttle position sensor (TPS) fails or reads erratically, causing the ECM to enter a limp/reduced-power mode that limits the vehicle to very low speed. This is a widely reported failure on the naturally aspirated 2.4L four-cylinder and 3.6L V6 engines and frequently appears alongside a 'Service StabiliTrak' message. The most commonly cited trouble code is P2135 (throttle/pedal position sensor voltage correlation). No NHTSA recall covers the throttle body; it is addressed through non-recall repair.
before.solution: Clean the throttle body if carbon buildup is the cause; if the throttle position sensor has failed the electronic throttle body assembly is replaced as a unit and the idle/throttle relearn procedure is performed.
symptoms: Sudden loss of acceleration / limp mode

before.title: 6T40/6T45 6-Speed Transmission Shudder and Harsh Shifts
before.description: The 2010-2017 Terrain uses the GM 6T40 (2.4L) and 6T45 (V6) 6-speed automatic transmissions, both of which suffer from torque converter shudder, harsh shifts, and solenoid failures. before.title: 10L80 10-Speed Transmission Harsh Shifting, Shudder and Rear-Wheel Lock-Up
before.description: The 10L80/10L90 ten-speed automatic exhibits harsh 1-2 upshifts when cold, steady-speed shudder around 40-70 mph, and a lag into Drive/Reverse that ends with a jolt. The failure point is valve-body wear and internal pressure leaks. In the worst case a transmission control-valve defect can cause a momentary rear-wheel lock-up; GM issued a large recall covering over 460,000 2020-2022 Silverado/Sierra/Tahoe/Suburban/Yukon/Escalade for this control valve. Multiple class-action suits have been filed and symptoms often surface between 40,000-60,000 miles.
before.solution: For the safety recall, dealers inspect and replace the transmission control valve (valve body) as required. For general shudder/harsh shifts, GM service procedures call for a transmission fluid flush with the correct Mobil 1 DEXRON-ULV (low-viscosity) fluid and, where wear is present, valve-body replacement; reprogramming the TCM with the latest calibration addresses many harsh-shift complaints. Confirm the transmission recall status by VIN before paying out of pocket.
symptoms: Harsh or clunky 1-2 upshift, especially when cold

before.title: 5.3L V8 Excessive Oil Consumption (AFM Oil Spray / Piston Rings)
before.description: The Active Fuel Management (AFM) 5.3L V8 burns oil at an abnormal rate, frequently a quart every 1,500-2,500 miles. The AFM pressure-relief valve in the valley sprays oil onto the cylinder walls when cylinders deactivate; combined with low-tension/coking piston rings and an oil-drawing PCV design, oil is drawn into the combustion chamber and burned. This is distinct from AFM lifter collapse - here the engine consumes oil, fouls plugs, and can run low enough to trigger misfires and low-oil warnings. A class-action settlement covered the LC9 5.3L piston-ring defect.
before.solution: GM's oil-consumption TSB fix installs updated pistons and rings and an AFM oil-deflector/shield in the valley. Common owner remedies: replace the PCV/updated valve covers, keep the oil topped up, and install an AFM/DOD delete or a catch can to stop the oil spray before ring damage occurs. If rings are already coked, a piston/ring job (or short block) is required. Verify oil-consumption class-action eligibility for affected VINs.
symptoms: Low oil level / low oil pressure warning
Blue smoke on startup or acceleration
Fouled spark plugs and rough idle / misfire

before.title: 6.2L L87 V8 Rod Bearing Failure and Loss of Propulsion
before.description: The 6.2L L87 V8 in 2021-2024 Yukons can suffer catastrophic engine failure from connecting-rod bearing damage. GM's own teardown analysis (Recall 25V-274 / N252494001) identified two supplier root causes: machining sediment left on the connecting rods and in the crankshaft oil galleries, and out-of-specification crankshaft dimensions/surface finish. The bearings spin and the engine can knock, seize, or throw a rod through the block, causing sudden loss of propulsion at speed. NHTSA logged thousands of loss-of-propulsion allegations and opened an investigation into post-recall failures. Roughly 82,000 Yukons are within the affected population.
before.solution: Under Recall 25V-274 GM inspects the engine; failed units get a full engine replacement (some receive GM remanufactured long blocks), and engines that pass inspection get a revised oil-fill spec switching from 0W-20 to thicker 0W-40 (GM dexos1 Gen 3), a new oil-fill cap, and a service-procedure update. Out of warranty, a rod-knock engine typically needs a complete engine or long-block replacement. Owners should have the recall performed at a GMC dealer at no charge and monitor for knocking or oil-pressure warnings.
symptoms: Deep knocking or rod-knock noise from the engine
Sudden loss of power or stalling while driving

before.title: 8L90 8-Speed Torque Converter Shudder
before.description: The 8L90 8-speed automatic transmission in 2015-2020 Yukon and Yukon XL suffers from widespread torque converter lock-up clutch shudder at light throttle between 25-50 mph. The clutch friction material degrades and contaminates the transmission fluid, causing the shudder to worsen over time. GM extended warranty coverage to 6 years/100,000 miles under Customer Satisfaction Program 18302. The fluid fix (Mobil 1 Synthetic LV ATF HP, GM 19417577) resolves early-stage cases; advanced cases require torque converter replacement. This is the same issue affecting all K2XX platform full-size GM SUVs and trucks.
before.solution: Full transmission fluid exchange with Mobil 1 Synthetic LV ATF HP (GM 19417577). Check Customer Satisfaction Program 18302 coverage. Torque converter replacement (GM 24288828) for persistent cases. Complete flush requires 17-20 quarts — ensure dealer uses full volume per TSB 18-NA-355.
symptoms: Shudder or vibration at light throttle 25-50 mph
Feels like driving on rumble strips at highway speed
Momentary slip when accelerating from a stop

before.title: AFM/DOD Lifter Collapse and Valvetrain Failure
before.description: The GMC Yukon 5.3L (L83, LC9, LMG) and 6.2L (L94, L86) V8 engines use Active Fuel Management (AFM) cylinder deactivation. The special collapsible AFM lifters on cylinders 1, 4, 6, and 7 fail prematurely, causing misfires, engine ticking, rough idle, and potential catastrophic damage. This is the single most reported mechanical failure on GMT900 (2007-2014) and K2XX (2015-2020) Yukon models. GM issued TSB 18-NA-077 acknowledging the issue. Yukon models used as daily drivers with lots of highway cruising (where AFM activates most) are most susceptible. The VLOM (Valve Lifter Oil Manifold) must also be replaced as it controls oil flow to AFM lifters.
before.solution: Replace all 16 lifters, VLOM (GM 12639516), and inspect camshaft lobes. AFM delete kit (Texas Speed or BTR) permanently eliminates the system. Range Technology AFM Disabler RA003B prevents AFM activation as a preventive measure. Change oil every 5,000 miles with Dexos1 Gen 2 full synthetic to protect lifters.
symptoms: Misfire codes P0300, P0301, P0304, P0306, P0307
Engine tick or tap at idle that worsens with load
Metal debris in oil (confirmed on drain plug inspection)
Vibration between 30-55 mph during V4 deactivation mode

before.title: Autoride Air Suspension Compressor and Air Bag Failure
before.description: Yukon and Yukon XL models equipped with Autoride (RPO Z55) or electronic suspension feature rear air springs and a compressor that commonly fail between 80,000-130,000 miles. The air spring bags crack from age and temperature cycling, causing the rear of the vehicle to sag overnight. The compressor burns out from running continuously to compensate for air spring leaks. Replacing OEM components and having them fail again is common — many owners convert to passive coil springs. Same system as Chevy Tahoe/Suburban and Escalade.
before.solution: Replace air springs and compressor (Arnott P-2793 compressor). Or install Arnott C-2835 / Strutmasters conversion kit to permanently eliminate air suspension with coil springs plus electronic bypass module. Conversion kits cost $400-700 and eliminate future air suspension failures.
symptoms: Rear of vehicle sagging overnight or after sitting
SERVICE RIDE CONTROL or AIR SUSPENSION message

before.title: Automatic 4WD Transfer Case Position Sensor / Encoder Motor Failure
before.description: On Autotrac electronic-shift 4WD Yukons the transfer-case encoder motor and its position sensor/selector switch fail, so the module can no longer confirm the range. The dash 4WD buttons flash, the truck won't shift between 2HI/4HI/4LO or gets stuck in one range, the Service 4WD light comes on, and codes such as C038D 'Range Actuator Position Not Learned' are stored. Worn encoder-motor contacts and corroded connector pins are typical causes.
before.solution: Diagnose whether the fault is the encoder motor, the position sensor/selector, or the transfer case control module. Common repairs: replace the transfer-case encoder/shift motor and the two/four-wheel-drive actuator position sensor (GM Genuine 84377721 / 84368196), and repin/repair the corroded connector. After replacement the actuator position must be relearned with a scan tool. Cleaning the dash 4WD switch contacts fixes some no-shift complaints.
symptoms: Won't shift between 2HI/4HI/4LO or stuck in range
Grinding/clicking from the transfer case during shift

before.title: Brake Vacuum Pump Failure Causing Hard Brake Pedal
before.description: The engine-driven mechanical vacuum pump that supplies power-brake boost can lose output when debris and oil sludge build up on its internal filter screen. Reduced vacuum means the brake booster no longer assists as designed, so the pedal becomes hard and stopping distances increase. GM Recall 19V-645 covers roughly 3.4 million 2014-2018 full-size trucks and SUVs including the 2015-2018 Yukon; GM reported 113 crashes and 13 injuries tied to the defect.
before.solution: Under Recall 19V-645 dealers reprogram the electronic brake control module to increase hydraulic brake assist when vacuum drops (free of charge). If the vacuum pump itself has failed, it is replaced with an updated ACDelco unit. Watch for the 'Service Brake Assist' message; drivers who lose assist should press the pedal firmly with steady pressure and get the recall completed. Verify the recall is closed by VIN at a GMC dealer.
symptoms: Hard/stiff brake pedal requiring extra force
Ticking noise from the engine bay

before.title: Cracked Dashboard Over Airbag and Instrument Panel
before.description: The one-piece molded dash pad splits and cracks, most often along the seam above the passenger airbag and over the instrument cluster. Owners attribute it to GM's switch from a multi-piece to a one-piece design with insufficient relief points and over-tightened mounting bolts, combined with heat/UV aging. Beyond the cosmetic damage there is a safety concern that a cracked seam can affect passenger-airbag deployment. A multi-state class action was filed in 2018 (E.D. Michigan); NHTSA declined a formal recall.
before.solution: The permanent fix is replacing the upper dash pad/instrument-panel trim pad (dealer quotes commonly around $1,500-$1,800 installed). Budget alternatives include a molded ABS dash cap/overlay bonded over the cracked pad or a carpeted dash cover. Parking in shade and using a windshield sunshade slows further cracking. There is no factory recall, so repair is owner-paid unless covered by an extended warranty.
symptoms: Cracks radiating from the passenger airbag seam
Split in the dash over the instrument cluster
Rattles or squeaks from the loose dash pad

before.title: Engine Overheat/Fail-Safe Mode from Thermostat and Coolant Temp Sensor
before.description: A worn or leaking factory thermostat that stays open (plus a failing engine coolant temperature sensor) prevents the engine from reaching normal operating temperature. The ECM interprets the low/erratic reading as a sensor fault and enters a protective fail-safe mode: the electric cooling fans run at full speed continuously, the temperature gauge may drop to zero or read erratically, the A/C compressor may be disabled, and fuel economy suffers. It is a common and well-documented complaint across 2015-2019 5.3L/6.2L trucks and SUVs.
before.solution: Diagnose whether the thermostat is stuck open or the ECT sensor has drifted. The usual repair is replacing the integrated thermostat housing and the engine coolant temperature sensor (GM Genuine ECT sensor 12608814) together with fresh DEXCOOL. Clearing the codes and confirming the engine reaches ~210F resolves the fans-on-full and disabled-A/C behavior. Address it promptly because the fail-safe also cuts A/C and hurts mileage.
symptoms: Cooling fans running at full speed constantly
Temperature gauge reads zero or fluctuates
A/C compressor won't engage / no cold air
Engine slow to warm up in cold weather

before.title: HVAC Blend Door Actuator Failure (Clicking Behind Dash)
before.description: The small electric blend-door actuators that control temperature and air-flow direction strip their internal plastic gears, producing a repetitive tapping/clicking noise from behind the radio or glovebox and causing the HVAC to blow the wrong temperature (e.g., stuck cold on the passenger side) or fail to change modes. It is one of the most common comfort complaints on the GMT900 Yukon and often affects more than one of the several actuators over the vehicle's life.
before.solution: Replace the failed actuator with a GM Original Equipment ACDelco unit - the passenger temperature actuator is ACDelco 15-72971 (GM 89018365 / 52402588; aftermarket cross Dorman 604-106). Before buying parts, pull the HVAC fuse for ~60 seconds to force a recalibration in case the fault is only a stuck cal. After replacement, reconnect the battery and let the system self-calibrate. OEM/ACDelco parts are strongly recommended because cheap aftermarket actuators have a high early-failure rate on this platform.
symptoms: Repetitive clicking/tapping behind the dash or glovebox
One side blows hot while the other blows cold
Temperature setting doesn't change actual output

before.title: Instrument Cluster Stepper Motor / Gauge Failure
before.description: The gauge cluster on 2003-2006 Yukons uses small stepper motors (the factory Switec/Juken X25.168-series) that wear out or jam. The speedometer, tachometer, fuel, or temperature needles twitch, flutter, stick, read wildly inaccurate, or peg at zero or maximum. A stuck or wrong speedometer is a safety and driveability concern and is one of the single most common electrical complaints on the GMT800 platform.
before.solution: Rebuild the cluster by replacing the failed stepper motors with updated X27.168 motors (a solder/DIY kit runs roughly $30-$60 plus new bulbs), or send the cluster to a specialist repair service (typically $120-$300 with a lifetime warranty). Full cluster replacement is possible but requires reprogramming the odometer/VIN, so a stepper-motor rebuild is the preferred, cheaper fix. Replacing all six motors at once is recommended since they fail in sequence.
symptoms: Speedometer or tach needle sticks, jumps, or reads wrong
Gauge pegged at zero or maximum

before.title: Intermediate Steering Shaft Clunk / Pop
before.description: A hallmark GMT800 complaint: a clunk or knock felt in the steering wheel and column when turning at low speed or driving over small bumps and rough pavement. The intermediate steering shaft (I-shaft) splines wear and lose lubrication, so the shaft binds and then releases with an audible/tactile pop. It is a comfort/annoyance issue rather than a loss-of-control safety defect, but it is extremely common and frequently returns after temporary fixes.

before.title: Power Running Board Motor Failure and Corrosion
before.description: The power retractable running boards available on 2015+ Yukon and Yukon XL are a common failure point. The electric motors and gearboxes corrode and seize, especially in salt-belt states. Boards get stuck in the out position (creating a road-clearance hazard and trip risk) or refuse to extend. The wiring harness connections at the running board motors corrode. GM has released multiple updated motor designs, but corrosion in the mechanical linkage pins also causes binding. Repair cost is $800-2,000 per side if both motors fail.
before.solution: Motor replacement (GM 84085689 updated motor). Lubricate pivot points and linkage pins with marine-grade grease annually. Dielectric grease on harness connectors. Some owners disable the system and lock boards in a fixed position to avoid ongoing failures.
symptoms: Running boards stuck in out position
Running boards not extending when door opens
Grinding or clicking noise when boards deploy
Service Running Boards message on DIC
Boards deploy on one side only
Boards extend but don't fully retract under the truck

before.title: Water Pump Weep-Hole Leak and Coolant Loss
before.description: The mechanical (belt-driven) water pump develops internal bearing and seal wear with age and mileage, then leaks coolant from the weep hole at the front-center of the engine. Left unaddressed the pump can drip DEXCOOL onto the ground, run the cooling system low, and cause overheating. It is a common wear item on the Gen IV/V small-block V8s used across the GMT900 and K2XX Yukon and typically shows up beyond ~90,000-120,000 miles.
before.solution: Replace the water pump (ACDelco Professional water pump for the applicable V8) with a new gasket, and refill with GM DEXCOOL. Because the serpentine belt, thermostat, and hoses are already accessed during the job, it is recommended to replace the thermostat and inspect the belt at the same time. Catch the weep-hole leak early to avoid an overheating event and possible head-gasket damage.
symptoms: Coolant puddle/drip at the front-center of the engine
Coolant seeping from the pump weep hole
Whining or grinding from a failing pump bearing

before.title: Dashboard Cracking and Warping from UV/Heat Exposure
before.description: The K2UC (2015-2020) generation Yukon XL dashboards develop cracks, warping, and delamination from UV exposure and heat cycling, particularly in southern states. Cracks typically originate near the defroster vents and passenger airbag seam and spread across the dash surface. The issue is covered under GM special coverage adjustment 14311 for some VINs, extending the warranty to 10 years. Beyond cosmetic concerns, severe cracking near the passenger airbag seam can affect proper airbag deployment.
before.solution: Check VIN eligibility for GM special coverage 14311 (free dashboard replacement at dealer, 10-year coverage). If not covered, dashboard replacement costs $800-2,000+ at a dealer. Aftermarket dashboard covers from DashMat or Coverlay are $150-300 alternatives that cover existing cracks. For a proper repair, the entire instrument panel must be removed (6-8 hours labor). Prevention: use a windshield sunshade and apply 303 Aerospace Protectant to the dash surface quarterly.
symptoms: Visible cracks spreading from defroster vent area
Shiny or sticky texture on dashboard
Cracks near passenger airbag deployment seam

before.title: Rear Liftgate Support Strut Failure
before.description: The Yukon XL rear liftgate gas struts lose their charge and fail to hold the heavy liftgate open, typically between 3-5 years regardless of mileage. The oversized liftgate of the XL model is significantly heavier than the standard Yukon, putting more stress on the struts. A failing strut allows the liftgate to slowly drop or slam closed, posing a head injury risk. In cold weather, weak struts fail more noticeably due to gas contraction.
before.solution: Replace both liftgate support struts as a pair (never replace just one). Strongarm 6262 or Sachs SG330090 are popular OE-equivalent replacements. The replacement takes about 15 minutes with a trim removal tool to pop the ball socket clips. Ensure the new struts are rated for the correct force (the XL requires higher-force struts than the standard Yukon). Power liftgate models should have the motor assembly inspected simultaneously.
symptoms: Liftgate does not stay open fully

before.title: Steering Column Lock Actuator Click and Binding
before.description: The electronic steering column lock (ESCL) actuator in 2015-2020 Yukon XL models develops a clicking, popping, or grinding noise when turning the steering wheel, particularly at startup. In some cases, the ESCL prevents the vehicle from starting entirely, displaying a "Steering Column Lock" message. GM issued TSB 16-NA-012 acknowledging the issue. The ESCL motor gear teeth strip or the position sensor misreads, causing the lock to partially engage or fail to release.
before.solution: Replace the electronic steering column lock actuator assembly (GM part 13501988). The replacement procedure requires disconnecting the battery, removing the lower steering column cover, and swapping the ESCL module. A Tech 2 or MDI scan tool relearn procedure must be performed after installation to program the new module to the BCM. Some owners have the ESCL permanently disabled via BCM programming at the dealer, though this may affect theft deterrent system operation.
symptoms: Clicking or popping noise from steering column on startup
Vehicle will not start — Steering Column Lock message
Grinding noise when turning the key or pressing start
Steering wheel feels temporarily locked after parking

before.title: Transmission Torque Converter Shudder (8L90/10L80)
before.description: The 8-speed (8L90) and 10-speed (10L80) automatic transmissions in the Yukon XL develop a torque converter clutch (TCC) shudder felt as a vibration or shake at light throttle between 25-50 mph. The shudder mimics driving over rumble strips. GM issued multiple TSBs (18-NA-355, 19-NA-193) and eventually reformulated the transmission fluid specification. The root cause is the TCC friction material interaction with the original Dexron HP fluid formulation.
before.solution: First-line fix: complete transmission fluid flush and fill with GM-approved Mobil 1 Synthetic LV ATF HP (Blue Label) — NOT the original red-label Dexron HP. This updated fluid resolves the shudder in approximately 80% of cases. If shudder returns within 30,000 miles of the fluid change, the torque converter requires replacement. Do NOT use aftermarket friction modifiers or additives — they void the GM powertrain warranty and can damage the transmission.
symptoms: Vibration or shudder at 25-50 mph under light throttle
Feels like driving over rumble strips
Vibration most noticeable in overdrive gears

before.title: Transfer Case Fluid Leak from Output Shaft Seal
before.description: Four-wheel-drive Yukon XL models with the NP263 (NQH) and NP246 transfer cases develop fluid leaks from the front and rear output shaft seals. The leak typically starts as a slow weep and progresses to a steady drip, leaving ATF spots on the driveway. If left unaddressed, the transfer case runs low on fluid, causing internal damage to the chain, sprockets, and bearings. The rear output seal is the most common failure point.
before.solution: Replace the leaking output shaft seal(s). The rear seal can be replaced with the transfer case in the vehicle by removing the rear driveshaft and prying out the old seal. The front seal requires more disassembly. Use only genuine ACDelco seals (ACDelco 24232325) as aftermarket seals have a higher failure rate on this application. Refill with Dexron VI ATF to the proper level. Inspect the output shaft for scoring — a scored shaft will destroy the new seal quickly.
symptoms: ATF dripping from transfer case area
Transfer case fluid low at service intervals
Grinding or whining noise from transfer case

before.title: Blend Door / HVAC Mode Actuator Failure Causing Incorrect Airflow or Temperature Control
before.description: Owners frequently report clicking behind the dash, air stuck on defrost or floor, or one side blowing the wrong temperature due to failed HVAC actuators. On Yukon XL models with front and rear climate systems, the mode and blend door actuators can strip gears or lose calibration over time. This is distinct from compressor failure and is a common repair on aging GMT800 SUVs.
before.solution: Use the HVAC self-diagnostic procedure or a scan tool where available, then identify whether the failed unit is the mode, temperature, or recirculation actuator. Replace the faulty actuator, inspect the door for binding, and perform actuator recalibration by pulling HVAC fuses or using the proper relearn procedure. Access can range from easy under-dash work to more involved dash disassembly depending on actuator location.
symptoms: air only blows from defrost vents
driver and passenger temperatures do not match
stuck on hot or cold air

before.title: Front Hub Bearing and ABS Wheel Speed Sensor Corrosion Causing Unwanted ABS Activation
before.description: GMT800 SUVs commonly develop corrosion under the front wheel speed sensors or wear in the hub bearing assembly, which alters the low-speed wheel speed signal. The result is unexpected ABS activation at parking-lot speeds, longer stopping distances, and a pulsating brake pedal even on dry pavement. GM documented this condition in service bulletins, and owners frequently report replacing hub assemblies to cure it.
before.solution: Scan ABS wheel speed data during a low-speed stop and compare left and right front sensor readings. If one sensor drops out, inspect for rust buildup under the sensor or excessive hub play; cleaning the sensor mounting surface may help temporarily, but many vehicles need a complete front hub/bearing assembly with integrated sensor. Clear ABS codes and road-test after repair.
symptoms: ABS activates at 3-10 mph on dry roads
brake pedal kicks back at low speed
longer stopping distance near a stop sign
grinding or humming from front wheel bearing

before.title: Fuel Pump Module Failure Leading to No-Start or Intermittent Stalling
before.description: In-tank fuel pump module failure is a common GMT800 problem, especially as mileage climbs or when vehicles are frequently run near empty. Owners report extended cranking, hard starts after sitting, sudden stalling, loss of power under load, or complete no-start conditions. The issue is well represented in owner reports and repair histories across 5.3L, 6.0L, and 8.1L applications.
before.solution: Verify fuel pressure at the rail and monitor pressure drop during key-on and cranking. If pressure is low or intermittent, replace the fuel pump module and inspect the electrical connector for heat damage; replacing the fuel filter at the same time is standard practice. On rusty vehicles, many owners choose to cut an access panel under the rear cargo area, though tank removal remains the factory method.
symptoms: engine cranks but will not start

before.title: Instrument Cluster Stepper Motor Failure Causing Inaccurate Gauges
before.description: 2003-2006 GMT800 full-size GM SUVs commonly suffer instrument cluster failures caused by defective stepper motors and related solder/joint issues inside the cluster. Owners report speedometers reading far too high or low, fuel gauges stuck on empty or full, and intermittent tachometer/oil pressure/voltmeter operation. GM issued a special coverage adjustment for many vehicles in this family because the problem was so widespread.
before.solution: Confirm the fault by comparing scan-tool data to gauge readings and checking for cluster self-test anomalies. The usual repair is instrument cluster rebuild or replacement with updated stepper motors; many owners use mail-in rebuild services. If mileage programming is required, use a qualified rebuilder or dealer-capable programming service.
symptoms: fuel gauge stuck on empty or full
oil pressure gauge pegged high or low

before.title: Intermediate Steering Shaft Clunk and Binding Over Bumps or During Turns
before.description: A very common GMT800 complaint is a clunk, knock, or slight bind felt through the steering wheel due to wear in the intermediate steering shaft. Owners often notice it at low speeds over small bumps, during parking maneuvers, or when transitioning on and off the brake. GM issued multiple service bulletins and revised shaft/lubrication procedures for this condition.
before.solution: Differentiate the noise from front suspension or steering gear play by checking the shaft for telescoping looseness and reproducing the clunk with the vehicle stationary. Depending on condition, the shaft can sometimes be lubricated per GM procedure, but replacement with the updated intermediate shaft is the more durable fix. After repair, verify steering wheel centering and absence of other front-end looseness.
symptoms: binding or notchy steering at low speed

before.title: Knock Sensor Water Intrusion Under Intake Causing Check Engine Light
before.description: The 4.8L, 5.3L, and 6.0L Vortec engines used in this generation commonly develop knock sensor faults because moisture collects in the valley beneath the intake manifold. Corrosion at the sensors or harness causes persistent P0327/P0332 codes, reduced spark advance, and occasional drivability complaints. This is a well-known GMT800 issue documented in GM service bulletins and owner forums.
before.solution: Scan for knock sensor codes, remove the intake manifold, and inspect both sensors, the sub-harness, and the rubber grommet seals. Replace both knock sensors and the harness together, clean the valley thoroughly, and reseal the sensor wells/grommets to prevent future water intrusion. Many technicians also verify no coolant leaks or cowl water leaks are contributing.
symptoms: recurring P0327 or P0332 after rain or washing
